title: How plants sense light, gravity and touch, and move in answer

summary.text: Put a cup of young moong shoots by a window, and by the next morning they all lean towards the glass. Nobody pushed them. Plants sense the world around them and respond to it, mostly by growing. A shoot grows towards the light. A root grows down, even when the seed is lying the wrong way up. A touch-me-not folds their leaves a second after you touch them. In this unit you test all three, and find out how a plant can move with no muscles.
summary.art: A steel katori of young moong shoots on a kitchen windowsill, every shoot leaning towards the bright glass.

intro.hook: Find a plant that grows by a window or on a balcony. Which way are their leaves facing: into the room, or out towards the light?
intro.text: Plants have no eyes and no muscles. Yet they know where the light is, which way is down, and when something touches them. To sense something means to notice it. To respond means to do something because of it. Plants do both, all day long. Before you read on, make a guess. If you turn a plant round so the leaves face away from the window, will they stay that way, or turn back? You are going to find out.
intro.art: A girl crouching by a balcony railing, looking closely at a money plant whose leaves all face out towards the sky.

outcomes: By the end I can say that plants sense light, which way is down, and touch, and that they respond to each one.
By the end I can show that a shoot bends towards the light, and turns back if the light comes from the other side.
By the end I can show that roots grow down, whichever way the sprout is lying.
By the end I can say how a touch-me-not responds to a touch, and that they fold their leaves at night too.
By the end I can say that most plants move by growing, so their movements are slow.
By the end I can guess first, give a reason, count what I see, and say what my test showed.

terms.meaning: To notice something, such as light, a touch, or which way is down.
terms.example: A moong shoot senses the light coming in from the window.
terms.art: A young moong shoot by a window, with soft lines of light coming in from one side.

terms.meaning: To do something because of what you sensed.
terms.example: A touch-me-not responds to a touch by folding their leaves.
terms.art: A finger touching a touch-me-not leaf, and the small leaflets folding up in pairs.

terms.meaning: The part of a young plant that grows up out of the soil: the stem and the first leaves.
terms.example: A moong shoot is a thin stem with two small leaves at the top.
terms.art: One moong seedling pulled out of the soil, with the shoot above and the white root below.

terms.meaning: A plant growing towards the light. 'Photo' means light. Say it 'foe-toe-TROPE-izm'.
terms.example: Moong shoots by a window bend towards the glass. That is phototropism.
terms.art: A row of small shoots in a cup, all curving towards a bright window.

terms.meaning: The pull of the Earth that makes things fall down.
terms.example: A dropped spoon falls to the floor because of gravity. Roots grow in the direction gravity pulls.
terms.art: A steel spoon falling towards a kitchen floor, beside a sprout whose root points down.

terms.meaning: The very end of a root. It senses which way is down.
terms.example: When a sprout lies on their side, the root tip curves round and grows down.

terms.meaning: A small plant whose leaves fold up when touched. Many people call them chhui-mui or lajjavati. In Malayalam they are thottavadi, and in Tamil thottal chinungi.
terms.example: Touch the tip of one leaf, and the small leaflets fold up, pair after pair.
terms.art: A touch-me-not plant with feathery leaves and small pink puffball flowers, one leaf folded shut.

terms.meaning: One of the small parts that together make one leaf on some plants.
terms.example: One touch-me-not leaf has many leaflets in pairs, like the teeth of a comb.
terms.art: One open touch-me-not leaf, with the pairs of small leaflets along each side.

terms.meaning: A message passed from one part to another.
terms.example: When you touch one leaflet, a signal runs along the leaf, and the next leaflets fold too.

explanations.concept: A shoot grows towards the light
explanations.context: This card explains the window test, where moong shoots leaned towards a window.
explanations.definition: Phototropism means a plant growing towards the light. The tip of a shoot senses which side the light comes from, and the shoot bends that way.
explanations.description: When light comes from one side, a growth chemical moves to the shady side of the stem. That side grows longer, so the shoot bends towards the light. In 1880, Charles Darwin and his son Francis covered the tips of grass seedlings, and the seedlings did not bend. So the tip is the part that senses the light.
examples: Moong shoots by a window lean towards the glass within a day.
A money plant on a windowsill turns their leaves to face outside.
Young sunflower plants turn to face the Sun as it crosses the sky.
explanations.art: A moong shoot drawn large, lit from the left. The shady right side of the stem is drawn a little longer, so the shoot curves to the left.

explanations.concept: Roots grow down, and shoots grow up
explanations.context: This card explains the root box, where sprouts lay pointing four different ways.
explanations.definition: Roots grow down, in the direction gravity pulls. Shoots grow up, away from it. This happens whichever way a seed is lying.
explanations.description: Inside a root tip are tiny heavy grains made of starch. They sink to the lowest side of each cell, like sand in a bottle, and that tells the root which way is down. The root then grows more on the upper side, so the tip curves down. Your ears have tiny crystals that do a similar job.
examples: A sprout laid with the root pointing up curves the root round to grow down.
A seed planted upside down still sends the root down and the shoot up.
A potted plant knocked onto their side slowly turns the shoot tips upwards again.
explanations.art: A root tip drawn as a row of cells, with tiny grains resting at the bottom of each cell, and an arrow pointing down.

explanations.concept: How a touch-me-not folds their leaves
explanations.context: This card explains what happens inside a touch-me-not leaf when you touch it.
explanations.definition: A touch-me-not folds when water moves out of the small swellings at the base of their leaflets.
explanations.description: At the base of each leaflet is a small swelling that holds water. A touch starts an electrical signal that runs along the leaf. Water quickly moves out of the cells on one side of each swelling, and the leaflets fold in a second or two. After about a quarter of an hour, water moves back and the leaflets open again. Every night the leaves fold by themselves too.
examples: A light touch on one leaflet folds a few pairs.
A firm tap folds the whole leaf, and the stalk drops down.
After dark, the leaves are folded even when nobody has touched them.
explanations.art: Two drawings side by side of a leaflet base: firm and full of water with the leaflet open, then soft on one side with the leaflet folded.

explanations.context: This card is about why a touch-me-not might fold their leaves. Scientists have ideas, but nobody is sure.
explanations.description: Nobody knows for certain why touch-me-not plants fold. Scientists have a few ideas, and more than one may be true.
examples: A folded plant looks thin and dry, so a goat or an insect may pass them by.
Folded leaves show the small prickles on the stems more clearly.
Folding may protect the leaves from heavy rain and strong wind.

perspectives.explanation: Folding protects the plant from animals that eat leaves. A plant that suddenly looks small and dry, with prickles showing, is less tempting.
Folding also protects the leaves from damage by heavy rain, strong wind or cold nights.

explanations.art: A goat sniffing at a touch-me-not whose leaves have just folded, showing the small prickles on the stem.

explanations.context: This card is about a question scientists still argue about.
explanations.description: Some scientists say plants feel, remember and decide. They point out that a root decides which way to grow, and that in one experiment touch-me-not plants stopped folding for a harmless drop and were still not folding weeks later. J.C. Bose, a scientist in Kolkata, measured electrical signals running through touch-me-not plants over 100 years ago. Many other scientists call these responses automatic. They say that sensing something is not the same as feeling it. Nobody knows for sure what being a plant is like.
examples: J.C. Bose recorded a small electrical signal each time a touch-me-not was touched.
A root grows round a stone and finds the way down again.
A climber's tendril coils round a stick that touches them.

perspectives.who: Scientists who study how plants behave
perspectives.explanation: Plants feel touch, light and gravity, remember what happened, and decide how to grow. Their signals work like messages in our own nerves.
Plants sense and respond, but this happens automatically, by chemicals and water moving. They do not use the words 'feel' or 'remember' for plants.

explanations.art: A touch-me-not plant in a pot beside a small notebook drawing of a wavy line, the electrical signal J.C. Bose recorded.

agreed.text: A shoot grows towards light that comes from one side.
agreed.evidence: Moong shoots by a window lean towards the glass within a day. Turn the cup round, and they bend back. Darwin's seedlings with covered tips did not bend, so the tip senses the light.

agreed.text: Roots grow down and shoots grow up, whichever way a seed is lying.
agreed.evidence: In the root box, sprouts laid pointing up, down, left and right all curved their roots to point down by the next day.

agreed.text: A touch-me-not folds their leaflets within seconds of a touch, and opens them again later.
agreed.evidence: Touch one leaf and watch: the leaflets fold pair after pair. Look again after about a quarter of an hour, and they are open.

agreed.text: Most plants move by growing, which is slow. A touch-me-not folds fast because water moves quickly out of cells.
agreed.evidence: A shoot takes hours to bend, so you only see it if you look again later. Time-lapse films, made by taking a photo every few minutes, show plants bending and turning all the time.

challenging.for: A plant stays in one pot and does not walk away. Most of the time you see no movement at all.
challenging.against: Plants move all the time, by growing. Shoots bend to the window, roots turn down, and leaves turn to face the light. A touch-me-not folds in a second. We miss most of it because it is slow.
challenging.context: This card is about a guess many people make.

challenging.claim: The light pulls the shoot towards the window.
challenging.for: The shoots end up pointing at the light, as if something tugged them there.
challenging.against: Light does not pull. The shoot's tip senses the light, and the shady side of the stem grows longer, so the shoot bends. The plant does the moving.
challenging.context: This card is about what makes a shoot bend.

challenging.claim: A sunflower in full bloom follows the Sun across the sky every day.
challenging.for: Young sunflower plants really do turn from east to west during the day, and back again at night.
challenging.against: In 2016, Stacey Harmer and her team in America found that once the big flower opens, most sunflowers stop turning and face east. East-facing flowers warm up faster in the morning and get more visits from bees.
challenging.context: This card is about a fact many people get half right.

challenging.claim: A touch-me-not can learn and remember.
challenging.for: Her plants stopped folding when they were dropped again and again with no harm. They still folded when shaken in a new way, so they were not just tired. Many still did not fold for the drop four weeks later.
challenging.against: Some scientists say this is not real memory, only a change in how the plant reacts. They want more tests.
challenging.context: This card is about a question scientists still argue about.

big_questions.q: A moong shoot has no eyes. How does the shoot know where the window is?
big_questions.hint: Think about which part of the seedlings Darwin covered.

big_questions.q: If you grew moong seeds in space, where nothing falls down, which way would the roots grow?
big_questions.hint: Think about what tells a root which way is down.

big_questions.q: A touch-me-not stopped folding for a harmless drop. Is remembering only for animals with brains?
big_questions.hint: Think about what the plant did differently after the first few drops.

big_questions.q: You turn your face to the Sun, and a shoot turns to the window. Do you and the plant sense the same world?
big_questions.hint: Think about what you use to sense light, and what a plant uses.

how_we_found_out.context: Does a touch-me-not fold every single time you touch them? This card tells the true story of a scientist who tested it.
how_we_found_out.story: Many people thought a touch-me-not folds their leaves every time they are touched, the way a bell rings every time you press it. In 2014, a scientist named Monica Gagliano tested this in Australia. She grew touch-me-not plants in pots. Then she dropped each pot gently, about 15 centimetres, onto soft foam, again and again. At first, the plants folded their leaves every time. After a few drops, many of them stopped folding. Were they just tired out? She tested that too. She shook the same plants from side to side, which was new to them. They folded at once. So they still had the energy to fold. They had stopped folding for the drop, because the drop did them no harm. Four weeks later, many of the plants still did not fold when dropped. They had remembered. Some scientists still argue about whether to call this learning and memory.
how_we_found_out.who: Monica Gagliano and her team, in Australia
how_we_found_out.wrong_idea: That a touch-me-not folds every single time, like a bell that rings whenever it is pressed. Gagliano's plants stopped folding for a harmless drop, still folded when shaken, and many kept this up for four weeks.
how_we_found_out.art: A row of potted touch-me-not plants on a lab bench, one pot being lowered gently onto a block of soft foam.

story.title: The Shoots That Turned Round
story.note: Nila, Siddharth and Ammamma are made up. Thottal chinungi is the Tamil name for the touch-me-not, and the plant grows wild on empty plots and roadsides in many Indian towns.
text: Nila was seven. She lived on the fourth floor of a building in Chennai, with her grandmother and her little brother Siddharth. Siddharth was five. Everyone called their grandmother Ammamma.
One Monday evening, Ammamma put a handful of green moong in a bowl of water. "Soak them tonight," she said. "Tomorrow, Nila, you can plant them."

On Tuesday, Nila pressed twelve swollen moong seeds into a katori of soil. She gave them two spoons of water. Then Ammamma turned an old steel vessel upside down over the katori. "Leave them in the dark for three days," she said.
On Friday, Nila lifted the vessel. Twelve thin shoots stood straight up, pale yellow, like tiny candles. Each one had two small folded leaves at the top.
"Now put them on the kitchen windowsill," said Ammamma.
Nila set the katori by the window. The light came in through the glass, from one side only.
On Saturday morning, Siddharth ran into her room. "Nila! Your plants are falling over!"
Nila hurried to the kitchen. The shoots were not lying down. They were leaning, all twelve of them, towards the window. They had turned a little green, too.
"The fan blew them over," said Siddharth.
"The fan is in the hall," said Nila. "There is no fan in the kitchen."
Siddharth thought hard. "Then the window pulled them."

Nila looked at the shoots for a long time. "Let's test it," she said. "If something knocked them over, they will stay bent the way they are. Let's turn the katori round, so they lean away from the window. Then we will see what they do."
She stuck a red bindi on the side of the katori that faced the glass. Then she turned the katori halfway round. Now the bindi faced the room, and every shoot leaned away from the light.
"Tomorrow we look," said Nila.
That evening, Siddharth peeped at the katori. "The tops are lifting up!" he said.

On Sunday morning, both of them stood at the windowsill. Every shoot had turned. The tips were pointing at the window again. Low down, each stem still leaned the old way. Higher up, it curved back towards the glass, like a wiggly letter S.
"They turned round by themselves," said Siddharth. "Nobody touched them."
"They sensed the light," said Nila. "Then they grew towards it."
"But they have no eyes," said Siddharth.

Ammamma came in with her coffee. "No eyes," she agreed. "The tip of each shoot senses the light. Then the shady side of the stem grows a little longer than the bright side. When one side grows longer, the stem bends. That is how a plant moves. Slowly, by growing."
Siddharth bent down and looked at one wiggly shoot. "So this low bend is from yesterday," he said slowly. "And the top bend is from today."
"Yes," said Nila. "The shoot keeps a record of where the light was."
"Can any plant move fast?" asked Siddharth.
Ammamma smiled. "When I was a girl in Palakkad, we had a plant called thottavadi near our well. Here in Chennai people call it thottal chinungi. Touch the leaves, and they fold up shut."
"Like a door?" asked Siddharth.
"Like a door," said Ammamma. "There is one growing on the empty plot near the bus stop."
After breakfast, the three of them walked down to the plot. Low among the grass grew a small plant with feathery leaves and fluffy pink flowers.

Nila showed Siddharth how to touch the tip of one leaf with one finger, very gently, and keep his hand away from the prickly stem. The tiny leaflets folded together, one pair after another, all the way along the leaf. Siddharth gasped.
"Now wait," said Nila. "Don't touch again. Let's see when they open."
They sat on the low wall and counted the buses. After seven buses, about a quarter of an hour, the leaflets had opened again.
On the way home, Siddharth was quiet. Then he said, "The thottal chinungi folds fast. The moong turns slowly. But they both know when something happens to them."
"They both sense," said Nila. "And they both respond."
That night, Nila drew the wiggly moong shoots in her notebook. Next to them she drew an arrow for yesterday's light and an arrow for today's.
story.epiphany: Nila sees that nobody moved the moong shoots. They sensed where the light was and turned themselves by growing, so the bends in their stems show where the light came from.
ask: Why did Nila turn the katori round?
If the fan had knocked the shoots over, what would Nila have seen the next morning?
The touch-me-not folds fast and the moong turns slowly. How are they the same?

experiments.title: The Window Test: will moong shoots turn back to the light?
experiments.context: In this experiment you grow moong shoots in the dark, so they stand straight. Then you put them by a window and count which way they lean. Then you turn the cup round, and find out what the shoots do next.
experiments.question: Which way do moong shoots grow when light comes from one side? If we turn the cup round, will they stay as they are, or turn back?
experiments.predict: Your straight shoots will stand by a window for a day. Which way do you think they will lean? Then we turn the cup round. What will they do then? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: We use one cup of shoots, with the same soil and the same water all through. The only thing we change is which side of the cup faces the window. A bindi marks the side that faced the glass first, so we always know how the cup was turned. We count every shoot, not just one, because one shoot on their own could be a fluke.

materials.item: whole green moong from the kitchen (sabut moong)
a small cup or katori, about as big as your fist
soil from a potted plant, enough to fill the cup, or wet cotton wool if you have no soil
a steel vessel, a bucket or a box, big enough to turn upside down over the cup
a bindi, a small sticker or a pen mark
water and a spoon
paper and a pencil, for drawing

schedule.what: In the evening, soak 15 moong in a bowl of water overnight.
Fill the cup with soil. Press 12 to 15 soaked moong just under the surface. Give 2 spoons of water. Cover the cup with the upside-down vessel.
Lift the vessel. Count the shoots and draw them. Mark the cup with a bindi. Put the cup by a window, bindi towards the glass. Guess what will happen.
Count and draw. Then turn the cup round so the bindi faces the room. Guess again.
Count and draw once more. Compare all three drawings and say what the shoots did.

experiments.record: Draw the cup three times: when it came out of the dark, after one day by the window, and the day after you turned it. Draw an arrow for where the light came from. Write how many shoots leaned to the window each time.

flow.do: 1. In the evening, put 15 whole moong in a bowl. 2. Cover them with water. 3. Leave them overnight.
flow.say: These moong seeds are going to drink water tonight. Tomorrow we plant them.
flow.kid: Put 15 moong in a bowl. Cover them with water. Leave them overnight.
flow.parent: Whole green moong sprouts reliably. Split moong dal will not grow. Start this four days before you want to do the window test.

flow.do: 1. Fill the cup with soil. 2. Your child presses 12 to 15 soaked moong just under the soil. 3. Give 2 spoons of water. 4. Turn the vessel upside down over the cup.
flow.say: We plant the moong and cover them. In the dark, they will grow straight up. Then we can see clearly if they bend.
flow.kid: Press the moong into the soil. Give 2 spoons of water. Cover the cup with the vessel.
flow.parent: Growing them in the dark matters. Shoots grown near a window lean before the test starts. In a warm room, the shoots are usually 3 to 6 cm tall after 3 days. If they are shorter than 2 cm, wait one more day.
flow.wait: Leave them for 3 days. On day 4, peep under the vessel and add a spoon of water if the soil is dry

flow.do: 1. Lift the vessel together. 2. Count the shoots and draw them. 3. Stick a bindi on the side of the cup. 4. Put the cup on a windowsill or a table right by a window, bindi towards the glass. 5. Ask for a guess and a reason.
flow.say: Look, they grew straight up in the dark. Now they will stay by the window until tomorrow. Which way do you think they will lean? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Lift the cover. Count the shoots. Draw them. Put the cup by the window, bindi to the glass. Which way will they lean? Say why.

ask.q: Why do you think they will lean that way?
good: Plants like light, so they will lean to the window.
They will stay straight, because nothing will push them.
I saw a plant on our balcony leaning out.

flow.parent: Choose a window that gives most of the room's daylight, so the light comes from one side. Keep the cup away from the fan. Write down your child's guess and reason, word for word. Don't say if it is right. The shoots are pale because they grew in the dark. They turn green in the light, too.
flow.wait: Leave the cup by the window until tomorrow

flow.do: 1. Look at the shoots together. 2. Count how many lean to the window, stand straight, or lean away. 3. Your child draws them. 4. Turn the cup halfway round, so the bindi faces the room. 5. Ask for a new guess.
flow.say: Count them with me. How many lean to the window? Now I turn the cup round. They all lean away from the light. What will they do by tomorrow? Why?
flow.kid: Count the shoots that lean to the window. Draw them. Turn the cup round. What will they do now? Say why.

ask.q: What do you think they will do now?
good: They will turn back to the window.
They will stay bent, because they are stuck that way.

flow.parent: Usually most shoots lean clearly towards the glass by morning, and many have turned green. If they are still straight, the window light may be weak. Move the cup closer to the glass and wait half a day more. Write down the second guess too.

check.q: After one day by the window, most of the moong shoots leaned towards the glass. What did they lean towards?
options: The light coming in
The wall of the room
The fan
check.why: The only thing on the window side was the light. The cup and the water were the same all round. So the shoots leaned towards the light.

flow.wait: Leave the cup turned round until tomorrow

flow.do: 1. Look and count again. 2. Your child draws them. 3. Put all three drawings in a row. 4. Ask what the shoots did, and how your child knows.
flow.say: What did the shoots do after we turned the cup? Look at your three drawings. What do you think made the shoots turn?
flow.kid: Count the shoots again. Draw them. Look at your three drawings. What did the shoots do? Why?

ask.q: Did the shoots stay bent the way we turned them?
good: No. They turned back to the window.
The tops turned back, but the bottoms stayed bent.

ask.q: Nobody touched them. So what made them turn?
good: They sensed the light and grew towards it.
They moved themselves.

flow.parent: Most shoots turn their tips back to the window within a day. Often the bottom of each stem still leans the old way, and the top curves back, like the letter S. The low bend has stopped growing, so it stays. Only the growing part near the top can bend again. Now read the explanation card on how a shoot bends.

check.q: We turned the cup round, and by the next day the shoots pointed at the window again. What does this show?
options: The shoots sense where the light is and grow towards it
Someone moved the shoots in the night
Shoots can only grow one way
check.why: Nothing else changed, only the side facing the light. The shoots turned back to the light by themselves, by growing.

experiments.title: The Root Box: which way will four roots grow?
experiments.context: In this experiment you lay four moong sprouts in a clear box, with their roots pointing up, down, left and right. You find out which way each root grows next.
experiments.question: If moong sprouts lie with their roots pointing four different ways, which way will each root grow?
experiments.predict: One root points up, one down, one left and one right. Which way will each root grow by tomorrow? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: All four sprouts are in the same box, on the same wet paper, in the same place. Only the way each sprout lies is different. We use sprouts with roots about as long as your fingernail, so that a bend is easy to see.
results_table: Way the root pointed at the start
Way the root tip points the next day

materials.item: moong sprouts with roots about 1 to 2 cm long (soak moong overnight, then keep them in a wet cloth for a day)
a clear plastic box with a lid, such as a sweets box or a takeaway box, or a clear glass tumbler with a plate on top
kitchen paper, tissue or a thin cotton cloth
water
a marker pen

schedule.what: Soak a spoonful of moong overnight.
Drain the moong and wrap them in a wet cloth for a day, until the roots are 1 to 2 cm long.
Set up the root box with four sprouts pointing four ways. Guess. Leave it standing up.
Look at each root tip. Draw them. Count how many point down.

experiments.record: Draw the box with the four sprouts as they were at the start. On the next day, draw them again, with the new part of each root.

flow.do: 1. Two days before, soak a spoonful of moong overnight. 2. Next morning, drain them and wrap them in a wet cloth.
flow.say: We are sprouting moong, the way we do for sundal or a salad. This time we need the little roots.
flow.kid: Soak the moong overnight. Then wrap them in a wet cloth.
flow.parent: In a warm room, roots are 1 to 2 cm long after about a day in the cloth. Many families already sprout moong this way, so you may have some ready.
flow.wait: Leave them for a day, until the roots are 1 to 2 cm long

flow.do: 1. Fold a wet paper and press it against one side of the box. 2. Your child slides 4 sprouts between the paper and the plastic. 3. Point one root up, one down, one left and one right. 4. Draw an arrow on the plastic beside each root, showing the way it points.
flow.say: Let's give each sprout a different way to point. One root up, one down, one left, one right. Draw an arrow for each one.
flow.kid: Slide four sprouts in. Point the roots up, down, left and right. Draw an arrow beside each one.
flow.parent: Keep the paper wet, but don't leave a puddle. The wet paper holds the sprouts against the plastic. If one slips, push the sprout back gently.

flow.do: 1. Close the lid. 2. Stand the box on one edge, so you can see the sprouts from the side. 3. Ask for a guess and a reason.
flow.say: Which way will each root grow by tomorrow? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Close the box. Stand it up. Which way will each root grow? Say why.

ask.q: Why do you think the root pointing up will grow that way?
good: Roots grow down, so the root will turn round.
The root will keep going up, because it is already pointing up.

flow.parent: Write down the guesses. Put the box in a warm place out of strong sun. The lid keeps the paper from drying out.
flow.wait: Leave the box standing up until tomorrow

flow.do: 1. Look at each root tip together. 2. Compare it with the arrow you drew. 3. Count how many tips now point down. 4. Your child draws them.
flow.say: Look at the tip of each root. Which way is it pointing now? How many point down?
flow.kid: Look at each root tip. Which way does it point now? Count how many point down.

ask.q: The root that pointed up: what did it do?
good: It curved round and grew down.
It made a hook shape.

flow.parent: Usually all four tips point down by the next day. The root that pointed up makes a hook. The one that already pointed down grows straight on. Then read the card on how a root knows which way is down. For more, turn the box a quarter of the way round and look again the next day.

check.q: A sprout lay with the root pointing up. The next day, which way did the root tip point?
options: Still up
Down
Sideways, towards the light
check.why: Roots grow in the direction gravity pulls. A root pointing up curves round until the tip points down.

activities.title: Leaf Watch: which way do the leaves face?
activities.context: This is a short looking activity to start the unit. You look at a plant that lives by a window or on a balcony, and count which way the leaves face.

materials.item: a potted plant that has stood by a window or on a balcony for at least a week, such as a money plant, tulsi or a curry leaf plant. If you have none, look at a plant in your building's stairway or a neighbour's balcony.
paper and a pencil

schedule.what: Look at the plant from the room side and the window side. Count the leaves facing each way.

activities.record: Draw the plant and the window. Draw a few leaves showing which way they face. Write two numbers: leaves facing the light, and leaves facing the room.

setup.art: A money plant in a pot on a windowsill, seen from inside the room, with most leaves turned out towards the glass.
setup.caption: 1. Look at the plant from inside the room.

setup.art: A child counting on her fingers while looking at the leaves, a tally on paper beside her.
setup.caption: 2. Count the leaves that face the light.

flow.do: 1. Stand with your child on the room side of the plant. 2. Look at the leaves together. 3. Ask what they notice.
flow.say: Look at this plant. Which way are the flat faces of the leaves turned? What do you notice? What do you wonder?
flow.kid: Look at the plant. Which way do the flat faces of the leaves point?

ask.q: What do you notice about the leaves?
good: Most of them face the window.
From here I see the backs of the leaves.
The stems lean out too.

flow.do: 1. Your child counts the leaves whose flat face points to the light. 2. Then they count the leaves whose face points into the room. 3. Write both numbers down.
flow.say: Let's count. How many leaves face the light? How many face the room?
flow.kid: Count the leaves facing the light. Count the leaves facing the room. Which number is bigger?
flow.parent: Most leaves usually face the light. Don't explain why yet. The window test will help your child find out.

flow.do: Ask for a guess and a reason, and write it down.
flow.say: Why do you think the leaves face that way? We will test it.
flow.kid: Why do the leaves face that way? Make a guess.
flow.think: Did the leaves grow that way, or did they turn?

activities.title: Touch-Me-Not Tests: what makes them fold? (if you can get a touch-me-not)
activities.context: This activity needs a touch-me-not plant, from a nursery or growing wild on an empty plot. You touch different leaves in different ways, count the pairs of leaflets that fold, and look again at night.

materials.item: a touch-me-not plant in a pot, or one growing wild nearby
a feather or a thin strip of paper
a spoon of water
a clock or a phone, to check the time
paper and a pencil

activities.safety: The stems have small prickles. Touch only the leaves, with one finger, and hold the pot, not the stem. Do not put any part of the plant in your mouth, and wash your hands afterwards.

schedule.what: Try four kinds of touch on four different leaves. Count the leaflet pairs that fold. Check when they open again.
After dark, look at the plant again without touching them.

activities.record: Make a table with four rows: blow, feather, drop of water, fingertip. Write how many pairs of leaflets folded each time. Draw the plant in the day and at night.

setup.art: A child blowing gently at one open touch-me-not leaf from a hand's length away.
setup.caption: 1. Blow gently on one leaf.

setup.art: A feather brushing the tip of a second leaf.
setup.caption: 2. Brush the tip of another leaf with a feather.

setup.art: A drop of water falling from a spoon onto a third leaf.
setup.caption: 3. Let one drop of water fall on a third leaf.

setup.art: One finger touching the tip of a fourth leaf, the leaflets folding pair after pair.
setup.caption: 4. Touch the tip of a fourth leaf with one finger.

flow.do: 1. Choose four leaves that are fully open. 2. Ask your child to guess which touch will fold the most leaflets.
flow.say: We will try four touches: a gentle blow, a feather, a drop of water and a fingertip. Which one will fold the most leaflets? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: You will try four touches. Which one will fold the most? Say why.
flow.parent: Use a different leaf for each touch, because a leaf that has just folded needs time to open again.

flow.do: 1. Your child tries each touch on its own leaf, one at a time. 2. After each one, count the pairs of leaflets that folded. 3. Write the number down.
flow.say: Blow gently from a hand's length away. Did any leaflets fold? Count the pairs. Now try the feather on the next leaf.
flow.kid: Try one touch on one leaf. Count the pairs that fold. Write the number. Then try the next touch.

ask.q: Did the folding stay where you touched, or did it travel?
good: It travelled along the leaf, pair after pair.
The next leaflets folded too, even though I did not touch them.

flow.parent: Many plants fold a lot for a fingertip and a drop of water, a little for a feather, and hardly at all for a gentle blow. Plants differ, so write down what yours really did. The folding running along the leaf shows a signal travelling.

flow.do: 1. Note the time. 2. Look at the fingertip leaf every 5 minutes, without touching. 3. Write the time when the leaflets are open again.
flow.say: Let's not touch them now. When do you think they will open again?
flow.kid: Don't touch. Look every 5 minutes. When are they open again?
flow.parent: Leaflets usually open again after about 10 to 20 minutes, sometimes longer. A plant in a cool or dim place may take more time.

check.q: You touched the tip of one leaf. Leaflets further along the leaf folded too. What does that show?
options: A signal travelled along the leaf
The wind folded them
They fold only when they are old
check.why: You touched only one place. The leaflets further along folded too, so a message must have passed along the leaf. That message is a signal.

flow.wait: Wait 10 to 20 minutes, looking every 5 minutes

flow.do: 1. After dark, take a torch to the plant with your child. 2. Look without touching. 3. Your child draws what they see.
flow.say: Nobody has touched the plant since this afternoon. Are the leaves open or folded?
flow.kid: Look at the plant at night. Don't touch. Are the leaves open or folded?
flow.parent: A touch-me-not folds their leaves every night and opens them in the morning. If the plant grows outside on a plot, go only with a grown-up, or skip this step and look early in the morning instead.

activities.title: Be a Young Sunflower: follow the torch
activities.context: This is an act-out with a torch. You play a young sunflower plant who turns to face the Sun all day. Then you play a grown sunflower with an open flower, who does something different.

materials.item: a torch or a phone light
a room you can make fairly dark
a paper with E written on it, for the east wall, and one with W, for the west wall, and sticky tape to fix them

schedule.what: Play a young sunflower following the torch from east to west and back at night. Then play a grown sunflower.

activities.record: Draw a young sunflower plant in the morning and in the evening. Draw a grown sunflower with the flower facing east.

setup.art: A child standing in the middle of a dim room with arms up like leaves, face turned to a torch held by a grown-up near a wall marked E.
setup.caption: 1. Morning: the torch shines from the east.

setup.art: The grown-up has walked over the top to the wall marked W, and the child has turned to face the torch.
setup.caption: 2. Evening: the torch reaches the west.

setup.art: The torch is off, and the child slowly turns back to face the wall marked E.
setup.caption: 3. Night: turn back to the east.

flow.do: 1. Find out which wall faces east, where the Sun rises. Use a phone compass, or ask where the morning Sun comes in. 2. Stick E on that wall and W on the opposite wall.
flow.say: The Sun rises in the east and sets in the west. Let's find our east wall.
flow.kid: Find the wall where the Sun comes up. Put E on it. Put W on the other side.

flow.do: 1. Your child stands in the middle, as a young sunflower plant. 2. Shine the torch from the E wall. 3. Walk slowly over to the W wall, holding the torch high. 4. Switch it off.
flow.say: You are a young sunflower plant. The Sun is coming up in the east. Turn your face slowly to follow it. Now it is night. What will you do?
flow.kid: You are a young sunflower. Turn your face to follow the torch. Turn slowly, like a plant.
flow.parent: Young sunflower plants really do face east in the morning and west in the evening. At night they turn back to face east, ready for sunrise. This was shown by Stacey Harmer and her team in America in 2016.

ask.q: When the torch went off, which way did you turn?
good: Back to the east, to wait for the morning Sun.

flow.do: 1. Now your child is a grown sunflower with a big open flower. 2. Shine the torch from E again, and walk across. 3. This time your child keeps facing east.
flow.say: Now you are a grown sunflower with a big flower. Grown sunflowers stop turning. They face east all day. Why do you think that helps?
flow.kid: Now you are a grown sunflower. Keep facing east, even when the torch moves.
flow.parent: Scientists found that east-facing flowers warm up faster in the morning sun, and bees visit warm flowers more. Accept any reason your child gives first.

check.q: Which sunflower turns to follow the Sun across the sky?
options: A young sunflower plant
A grown sunflower with a big open flower
Both, all their life
check.why: Young sunflower plants turn from east to west and back at night. Once the big flower opens, most sunflowers stop turning and face east.

activities.title: Which Way Is Down? Find it with your eyes shut
activities.context: A root knows which way is down. So do you. In this short activity you find the floor with your eyes shut, and learn what helps you.

materials.item: a bed, a mat or a soft rug to lie on

schedule.what: Lie in different ways with your eyes shut and point to the floor each time.

activities.record: Draw yourself lying three ways, with an arrow pointing to the floor each time.

setup.art: A child lying on her side on a mat with her eyes shut, pointing at the floor.
setup.caption: 1. Lie on your side. Shut your eyes. Point to the floor.

setup.art: The same child lying on her back with eyes shut, pointing down at the mat beside her.
setup.caption: 2. Roll over. Point to the floor again.

flow.do: 1. Your child lies on their side on the mat, eyes shut. 2. They point to the floor. 3. They roll onto their back and point again, then onto the other side.
flow.say: Shut your eyes. Point to the floor. Now roll over. Point to the floor again. How did you know?
flow.kid: Lie down. Shut your eyes. Point to the floor. Roll over and point again.

ask.q: How did you know where the floor was?
good: I could feel it in my head.
I felt the bed under me.

flow.do: Tell your child about the tiny crystals in our ears, and link them to the root box.
flow.say: Deep inside each ear are tiny crystals. When you tilt your head, they press on tiny hairs, and your brain knows which way is down. A root tip has tiny heavy grains that sink to the bottom of each cell. Both of you sense gravity.
flow.kid: Your ears have tiny crystals. They help you know which way is down. A root tip has tiny heavy grains that do the same.
flow.parent: The crystals sit in a small part of the inner ear. The grains in a root tip are made of starch. Both sense the pull of gravity.

games.title: Sense and Respond: a pairs game
games.context: This is a memory game about what plants sense and what they do about it. You turn over two cards at a time and look for a pair: something a plant senses, and the way the plant responds.

printables.title: 16 cards to cut out: 8 sense cards and 8 respond cards
items: Light comes in from the window onto a moong shoot.
The moong shoot bends towards the window.
A sprout is lying with the root pointing up.
The root tip curves round and grows down.
A finger touches the tip of a touch-me-not leaf.
The leaflets fold up, pair after pair.
Night comes.
The touch-me-not folds their leaves until morning.
The Sun moves across the sky over a young sunflower plant.
The young sunflower plant turns from east to west.
A climber's tendril touches a stick.
The tendril coils round the stick.
The soil is wet on one side of the pot.
The roots grow towards the wet side.
A potted plant is knocked over and lies on the floor.
The shoot tips slowly turn upwards again.

rules: If a child cannot read yet, draw a small sketch on each card before you play.
Mix the cards and lay them face down in 4 rows of 4.
On your turn, turn over two cards and read them aloud.
A pair is one card that says what a plant senses, and the card that says how that plant responds. Each sense card has only one response card that goes with it.
If you have a pair, say why the two cards go together. If the other players agree, keep the pair and play again.
If they are not a pair, turn them back face down. The next player has a turn.
When all the cards are taken, the player with the most pairs wins. If two players have the same number, they both win.

setup.art: Sixteen small cards face down in four rows of four on a floor mat.
setup.caption: 1. Lay the 16 cards face down in 4 rows of 4.

setup.art: A girl turning over two cards, one showing a window with light and one showing a bending shoot.
setup.caption: 2. Turn over two. Is it a sense and its response?

flow.do: 1. Cut out the cards together. 2. If your child cannot read yet, they draw a small sketch on each card. 3. Lay the cards face down in 4 rows of 4.
flow.say: Let's lay the cards face down. Every sense card has one response card that goes with it.
flow.kid: Cut out the cards. Lay them face down.

flow.do: 1. Take turns as the rules say. 2. When someone finds a pair, ask them why the two cards go together.
flow.say: You found light from the window and a bending shoot. Why do they go together?
flow.kid: Turn over two cards. Is it a pair? Say why they go together.

check.q: A sprout is lying with the root pointing up. Which card goes with it?
options: The root tip curves round and grows down.
The leaflets fold up, pair after pair.
The shoot bends towards the window.
check.why: A root senses which way is down, and curves round to grow that way. Folding leaflets go with a touch, and a bending shoot goes with light.

flow.do: Lay all the pairs out. Sort them into three groups: light, down, and touch. Put any pair that fits none in a fourth group.
flow.say: Which pairs are about light? Which are about which way is down? Which are about touch?
flow.kid: Sort the pairs into light, down and touch. Which pairs are left over?
flow.parent: The night pair and the wet soil pair fit none of the three groups; put them in the fourth group. The knocked-over pot goes with 'down'.

games.title: Plant Says: a moving game
games.players: 2 or more people: one is the caller, the others are plants
games.context: This is a moving game, a little like Simon Says. Each player is a plant. The caller reads a card, and the players respond the way a real plant would.

items.f: The window is on your left.
items.b: Lean slowly to the left, counting to five.

items.f: The window is on your right.
items.b: Lean slowly to the right, counting to five.
Slowly turn back to face the window.

items.f: You are lying on your side.
items.b: Slowly curve your feet, your roots, round to point at the floor.
Touch-me-not: fold your arms in fast!
Touch-me-not: fold your arms and keep still.

items.f: Morning, and nobody has touched you for a while.
The Sun rises in the east.
items.b: Young sunflower: turn your face to the east wall.

rules: Players stand up. Hands held together above your head are your shoot. Your feet are your roots. Open arms are touch-me-not leaves.
The caller reads the front of a card aloud. Players move.
The caller then reads the back. Anyone who moved the wrong way, or too fast, sits down for the next card, then joins in again.
Light and gravity moves must be slow, counting to five, because most plants move by growing. Only the touch-me-not fold is fast.
The game ends when all 8 cards have been read. Everyone who moved the right way every time wins. Then swap, and play again.

setup.art: Three children standing with their hands together above their heads, leaning slowly towards a window.
setup.caption: 1. Hands up for a shoot. Lean slowly to the light.

setup.art: A child quickly folding her arms across her chest as the caller reads a card.
setup.caption: 2. A touch: touch-me-not players fold fast.

flow.do: Read the rules aloud. Show the shoot, the roots and the touch-me-not arms.
flow.say: You are all plants. Your hands are your shoot and your feet are your roots. Most plant moves are slow.
flow.kid: You are a plant. Hands up for your shoot. Feet are your roots.

flow.do: 1. Read the cards one at a time, in any order. 2. After each one, ask a player why a plant moves that way.
flow.say: The window is on your left. Go! Why did you lean slowly?
flow.kid: Listen to the card. Move like a plant. Slow for light, fast for a touch.

check.q: In Plant Says, why must the light moves be slow?
options: A shoot bends by growing, and growing is slow
Plants are tired
Light moves slowly
check.why: A shoot bends because one side grows longer than the other. Growing takes hours. A touch-me-not folds fast because water moves quickly out of cells.

flow.do: Ask which move was the only fast one, and why.
flow.say: Which move was the only fast one? Why can a touch-me-not move so fast?
flow.kid: Which move was fast? Why?

projects.title: Turn the Pot: a week with a windowsill plant
projects.context: In this one-week project you turn a potted plant round, so the leaves face the room instead of the window. Then you draw the plant every few days and count the leaves facing the light.

materials.item: a potted plant that lives by a window or on a balcony, such as a money plant, tulsi or a mint pot
a bindi or a small sticker
paper and a pencil

schedule.what: Count the leaves facing the light. Draw the plant. Stick a bindi on the window side of the pot. Turn the pot halfway round.
Count the leaves facing the light again. Draw the plant.
Count and draw once more. Put the four drawings in a row and talk about what changed.

projects.record: Make a table with the day and the number of leaves facing the light. Keep your four drawings in order.

setup.art: A tulsi pot on a windowsill with a bindi on the side facing the glass, being turned halfway round by a child.
setup.caption: 1. Mark the window side. Turn the pot round.

setup.art: The same tulsi a week later, with the leaves turned back to face the window.
setup.caption: 2. Draw and count every few days.

flow.do: 1. Your child counts the leaves facing the light and draws the plant. 2. Stick a bindi on the window side of the pot. 3. Turn the pot halfway round. 4. Ask for a guess.
flow.say: Now most leaves face the room. What will they do in a week? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Count the leaves facing the light. Draw the plant. Turn the pot round. What will the leaves do? Say why.
flow.wait: Leave the pot turned round. Look again in 2 days

flow.do: On day 3 and day 5, your child counts the leaves facing the light and draws the plant.
flow.say: Count the leaves facing the light. Is the number bigger or smaller than last time?
flow.kid: Count the leaves facing the light. Draw the plant. Is the number going up?
flow.parent: Leaves usually twist slowly on their stalks to face the light again, and new tips bend towards it. A money plant can take a week or more. If you see no change by day 8, keep going to day 14.

flow.do: 1. Count and draw one last time. 2. Put the drawings in a row. 3. Ask what changed, and what made it change.
flow.say: Look at your drawings in order. What did the plant do? Nobody turned the leaves. So who did?
flow.kid: Put your drawings in a row. What did the leaves do? Who turned them?

check.q: You turned a money plant pot round. A week or more later, most leaves faced the window again. Why?
options: The plant sensed the light and turned the leaves towards it
The wind blew the leaves round
The leaves fell off and new ones grew
check.why: The plant senses where the light comes from and slowly turns the leaves to face it, by growing. That way each leaf catches more light to make food.

challenges.title: Straight Shoots by a Window
challenges.context: In the window test, moong shoots leaned towards the glass. This challenge asks you to help shoots grow straight up while they stay by the window.
challenges.problem: Your cup of moong shoots must stay by the window, and you must not turn the cup. Help the shoots grow straight up instead of leaning.
constraints: The cup stays in the same place by the window.
You may not turn the cup.
The shoots must still get light.
Use only things from home: paper, card, foil, a steel plate, a box, tape.
materials: a cup of young moong shoots, grown in the dark as in the window test (start at least 5 days ahead), and a second cup to leave with no help, if you have grown two
kitchen foil, if you have some
general: Stand a white card or a sheet of foil behind the cup, on the room side, so light bounces back onto the shady side of the shoots.
Cover the cup with a box that has a hole only in the top, so the light comes from above.
creative: Tilt a shiny steel plate behind the cup so it sends window light onto the room side.
Make a paper tube around the cup, open at the top, like a chimney.
challenges.your_turn: Design your own way. Leave it for a day, then count how many shoots stand straight. Was your idea better than no help at all?

setup.art: A cup of moong shoots by a window with a sheet of foil standing behind the cup on the room side.
setup.caption: 1. Try a shiny card behind the cup.

setup.art: A cardboard box over a cup of shoots by a window, with a round hole cut only in the top.
setup.caption: 2. Or try a box with a hole in the top.

flow.do: 1. Read the problem together. 2. Ask your child why the shoots lean. 3. Ask for ideas before showing anything.
flow.say: The shoots lean because light comes from one side. How could we make them grow straight, without moving or turning the cup?
flow.kid: The shoots lean to the light. How can you make them grow straight? Think of an idea.

good: Put a light on the other side.
Make the light come from the top.
Put something shiny behind them.

flow.do: 1. Your child builds their idea. 2. A grown-up helps with any cutting. 3. Keep one cup with no help, if you have enough shoots, to compare.
flow.say: Build your idea. If we have two cups, we leave one with no help, so we can compare.
flow.kid: Build your idea. Ask a grown-up to help you cut.
flow.parent: A box with a hole in the top usually works best, because the light then comes from above. A shiny card behind the cup usually makes the lean smaller, but not gone.

flow.do: 1. Count the straight shoots in each cup. 2. Talk about which idea worked best, and why.
flow.say: How many shoots stand straight with your idea? How many in the cup with no help?
flow.kid: Count the straight shoots in each cup. Which idea worked best?

check.q: Why does a box with a hole in the top help the shoots grow straight?
options: The light now comes from above, so no side is shady
The box keeps the shoots warm
The box pushes the shoots up
check.why: A shoot bends when one side gets less light. With light from straight above, both sides get the same light, so the shoot grows straight up.

items.p: Why did we grow the moong in the dark before the window test?
opts: So all the shoots stood straight before the test
So the shoots grow faster in the dark
items.why: Shoots grown near a window lean before the test starts. In the dark they stand straight, so any lean we see later comes from the window light.
items.context: This question is about the window test. You grew moong shoots in the dark, put them by a window, and later turned the cup round.

items.p: Draw your cup of moong shoots after one day by the window. Draw an arrow to show where the light came from.
items.a: The cup with the shoots leaning towards the window, and an arrow from the window to the shoots.
items.why: A strong drawing shows the shoots leaning the same way the light came from, as in the child's own test.
items.context: This question is about the window test. You grew moong shoots in the dark, put them by a window, and later turned the cup round.

items.p: A root grows down even when the sprout is lying with the root pointing up.
items.why: True. In the root box, the root that pointed up curved round and grew down.
items.context: This question is about the root box. You laid four moong sprouts in a clear box, with their roots pointing up, down, left and right.

items.p: Draw a line from what the plant sensed to what the plant did.
pairs: A sprout lying on its side
items.why: Each response matches what the plant sensed: light, gravity, touch, or the dark of night.

items.p: A touch-me-not folds fast because ____ moves quickly out of cells at the base of each leaflet.
items.why: Plants without muscles can still move fast. Water leaving the cells makes the swelling soft, and the leaflets fold.

items.p: Say out loud, and a grown-up writes it down: we turned the cup round. Why did the shoots bend back towards the window?
items.a: Because they sensed the light on the window side and grew towards it again.
items.why: A strong answer says the shoots sensed where the light was and turned themselves by growing. Nobody moved them.
items.context: This question is about the window test. You grew moong shoots in the dark, put them by a window, and later turned the cup round.

items.p: Three of these plant movements are slow and take hours. Which one is fast?
opts: A shoot bending to a window
A money plant turning their leaves
items.why: A touch-me-not folds in a second or two, because water moves quickly out of cells. The others happen by growing, which takes hours.

items.p: Farhan, a boy in Class 2, and his sister Reshma, in Class 3, look at the leaning moong shoots.

views.says: The window pulled the shoots towards it.
The shoots grew towards the light by themselves.

items.ask: Who do you agree with? Give one reason from your own test. Then say one thing the other person noticed that is true.
items.a: A strong answer picks a side with a reason from the test, such as 'when we turned the cup, they turned back by themselves', and says Farhan was right that the shoots end up pointing at the window.
items.why: Light does not pull. But Farhan noticed something real: the shoots do end up pointing at the window. Reshma's view explains why.
items.context: This question is about the window test. You grew moong shoots in the dark, put them by a window, and later turned the cup round.

items.p: Label the moong seedling: shoot tip, stem, root, root tip.
a: the top with two small leaves: shoot tip
the thin part above the soil: stem
the white part in the soil: root
the very end of the root: root tip
items.why: The shoot tip senses light. The root tip senses which way is down.
items.art: A drawing of one moong seedling with the soil line marked, and four empty label lines.

items.p: A moong shoot bends towards the light because the ____ side of the stem grows longer.
items.why: The side of the stem away from the light grows more, so the stem curves towards the light.
items.context: This question is about the window test. You grew moong shoots in the dark, put them by a window, and later turned the cup round.

items.p: Put the steps of the root box in order.
items: Slide in four sprouts, pointing four ways
Close the box and stand it up
Wait one day
Look which way each root tip points
items.why: First set up the sprouts, then close the box and wait, and only then look at what the roots did.
items.context: This question is about the root box. You laid four moong sprouts in a clear box, with their roots pointing up, down, left and right.

items.p: Selvi, a girl in Madurai, lays a sprout with the root pointing sideways, to the left. Where will the root tip point the next day?
items.why: Roots grow in the direction gravity pulls, so the tip curves down. Picking 'up' mixes up roots with shoots.
items.context: This question is about the root box. You laid four moong sprouts in a clear box, with their roots pointing up, down, left and right.

items.p: Sort these plant movements: fast (in seconds) or slow (hours or days).
items: touch-me-not leaflets folding
Fast
moong shoot bending to a window
Slow
root curving down
Slow
Venus flytrap shutting on an insect
Fast
young sunflower turning from east to west
Slow
items.why: Most plants move by growing, which is slow. A touch-me-not moves fast by moving water in their cells. A Venus flytrap also shuts in about a second.

items.p: Why might a touch-me-not fold their leaves when an animal brushes past? Give one idea.
items.a: A folded plant looks small and dry, so the animal may not eat them. Or the prickles show more.
items.why: Nobody knows for sure. A strong answer gives one idea and a reason. Saying 'nobody knows for sure' is also a strong answer.

items.p: Draw a moong shoot after one day by the window, then the same shoot one day after the cup was turned round.
items.a: First a shoot leaning towards the window. Then a shoot bent like an S, the bottom leaning away and the top curving back to the window.
items.why: The low part of the stem has stopped growing and stays bent. The growing top bends back to the light.
items.context: This question is about the window test. You grew moong shoots in the dark, put them by a window, and later turned the cup round.

items.p: A plant needs muscles to move.
items.why: False. A shoot bends by growing more on one side. A touch-me-not folds by moving water out of cells. Neither uses muscles.

items.p: Tara, a girl in Kolkata, touched one touch-me-not leaf and 12 pairs of leaflets folded. On another leaf, 9 pairs folded. How many pairs folded in all?
items.why: 12 + 9 = 21. Count on 9 from 12: 13, 14 and so on up to 21.
items.context: This question is about the touch-me-not tests. You touched touch-me-not leaves in different ways and counted the pairs of leaflets that folded.

items.p: Gauri, a girl in Pune, and her cousin Arjun, a boy in Class 2, are talking about a touch-me-not.

views.says: A touch-me-not feels a touch, just as I do.
A touch-me-not just reacts, like a door that shuts when you push it.

items.ask: Who do you agree with? Give one reason. Then say what the other person might answer back.
items.a: A strong answer picks a side with a reason, for example that touch-me-not plants stopped folding for a harmless drop in one experiment, which a door never does. Then it gives the other side's best point.
items.why: Scientists still argue about this. Some say plants feel and remember. Many call it an automatic reaction. Both sides use real evidence.

items.p: Tiny heavy grains in a root tip sink to the ____ side of each cell, so the root knows which way is down.
items.why: Whichever way the root lies, the grains sink to the lowest side, like sand in a bottle.

items.p: Label the touch-me-not leaf: leaflets, leaf stalk, swelling at the base.
a: the small parts in pairs: leaflets
the long part that holds the leaf: leaf stalk
the small bump where the stalk joins the stem: swelling at the base
items.why: The swelling at the base is full of water. When water moves out of one side, the leaf droops.
items.art: A drawing of one touch-me-not leaf on a stem, with three empty label lines.

items.p: Many people think a sunflower in full bloom follows the Sun all day. What would you look at, and when, to find out?
items.a: Look at a sunflower with an open flower in the morning, at midday and in the evening, and see which way the flower faces each time.
items.why: A strong answer looks more than once, at different times of day. Scientists who did this found that most open sunflowers face east all day.

items.p: Darwin covered the tips of grass seedlings with tiny caps. Then the seedlings did not bend to the light. What does this show?
opts: Grass grows only in the dark
items.why: Only the tip was covered, and the bending stopped. So the tip is where the light is sensed.

items.p: Anu, a girl in Kochi, and her aunt Leela, a plant scientist, look at the root box.

views.says: The root decided to grow down.
Heavy grains sank in the root tip, so the root grew down. That is how it works.

items.ask: Who do you agree with? Give one reason. Can both be right at once?
items.a: A strong answer picks a side with a reason, and thinks about whether knowing how something works also tells us whether the root decided.
items.why: Leela describes how the root senses gravity. Anu describes what the root does with it. Some scientists say the root decides where to grow; others use only words like Leela's.

items.p: Imagine you turn the root box a quarter of the way round every day for three days. Draw the shape you think one root will make.
items.a: A zigzag or a curl: each day the tip bends to point down again.
items.why: Each time the box turns, the root tip senses the new 'down' and curves towards it, so the bends add up.
items.context: This question is about the root box. You laid four moong sprouts in a clear box, with their roots pointing up, down, left and right.

items.p: If you turn a potted plant round on a windowsill, the leaves slowly turn back to face the window.
items.why: True. The plant senses which side the light comes from and turns the leaves to face it, over days or weeks.

items.p: Lakshmi, a girl in Hyderabad, puts a cup of moong shoots by a window. She turns the cup a little every hour, all day long. Which way will the shoots lean in the evening?
items.why: Each side of the cup faces the light in turn, so no side stays shady for long. The shoots grow mostly straight. Picking 'strongly towards the window' forgets that the cup kept turning.

items.p: Sort by what the plant sensed: light, gravity or touch.
items: shoot bends to the window
Light
root turns down
Gravity
touch-me-not folds
Touch
tendril coils round a stick
Touch
root bends again when the box is turned
Gravity
young sunflower turns from east to west
Light
items.why: Bending to a window and following the Sun are about light. Roots turning down are about gravity. Folding and coiling are about touch.

items.p: Why are most plant movements too slow for us to see, even if we watch closely?
items.a: Because most plants move by growing, and growing takes hours or days.
items.why: A strong answer links the slow movement to growing. A touch-me-not is fast because they use water, not growing.

items.p: A root bends down because the ____ side of the root grows more.
items.why: When the top side grows longer than the bottom side, the root curves downwards.

items.p: A friend says, 'Plants just sit there. They never move.' What would you tell your friend? Use something you have seen.
items.a: Plants move by growing: a shoot bends to a window, a root turns down, a touch-me-not folds in a second. We miss most of it because it is slow.
items.why: A strong answer gives one example the child saw, such as shoots leaning in the window test, and says that most plants move slowly, by growing.

quiz.p: You put a cup of straight moong shoots by a window. The next day, which way will they lean?
quiz.why: The shoots sense the light and grow towards it. Picking 'fall flat' may mean thinking the shoots get knocked over, but they stand up, only leaning.

quiz.p: Which part of a shoot senses the light?
quiz.why: Darwin covered the tips of seedlings, and they stopped bending to the light. Picking 'roots' mixes up light with gravity.

quiz.p: A moong sprout lies with the root pointing up. What will the root do?
quiz.why: Roots grow in the direction gravity pulls. Picking 'keep growing up' means thinking a root just carries on the way it points.

quiz.p: What helps a root tip know which way is down?
opts: Tiny heavy grains that sink to the lowest side of each cell
quiz.why: The grains always sink to the lowest side, whichever way the root lies. Roots have no eyes, so 'sees the floor' cannot be right.

quiz.p: What does a touch-me-not do when you touch the tip of one leaf?
opts: The leaflets fold up, pair after pair
quiz.why: A signal runs along the leaf, water moves out of cells at the base of each leaflet, and the leaflets fold.

quiz.p: When else does a touch-me-not fold their leaves, with nobody touching them?
quiz.why: A touch-me-not folds their leaves every night and opens them in the morning.

quiz.p: How does a moong shoot bend towards the light?
opts: The shady side of the stem grows longer, so the stem curves
The plant walks on their roots
The wind blows the shoot over
quiz.why: The plant sends a growth chemical to the shady side. That side grows longer, so the stem curves towards the light.

quiz.p: Why can't we see a moong shoot bending, even if we stare at the shoot?
opts: The shoot bends by growing, and growing is slow
The shoot moves only when nobody is looking
quiz.why: Growing takes hours. We see the bend only if we look again later, or watch a time-lapse film.

quiz.p: Ravi, a boy in Bhubaneswar, turned his money plant pot round, so the leaves faced the room. What will happen in a week?
opts: The leaves slowly turn back to face the window
quiz.why: The plant senses which side the light comes from, and turns the leaves to face it again.

quiz.p: In one experiment, a scientist dropped touch-me-not plants gently, again and again, with no harm. What happened after a few drops?
opts: Many stopped folding their leaves for the drop
quiz.why: Many stopped folding for the drop. They still folded when shaken in a new way, so they were not just tired. Scientists still argue about whether to call this learning.

quiz.p: Divya, a girl in Class 2, guessed the moong shoots would lean to the window. What is the best way to check her guess?
opts: Put shoots by a window and look the next day
Ask a friend what they think
quiz.why: A test with real shoots shows what really happens. Asking or guessing again cannot tell us.

quiz.p: Which of these do plants sense?
quiz.why: Plants sense light, which way is down, touch, water and more. Picking 'nothing at all' may mean thinking that a plant that stays still senses nothing.

applications: Gardeners turn pots on a windowsill every few days, so the plant grows straight instead of leaning to one side.
Farmers sow seeds without worrying which way up they land, because roots find their way down and shoots find their way up.
On the International Space Station, where nothing falls, plants have no 'down' to sense. Their shoots grow towards the light instead.
Climbers like bottle gourd and beans are given a stick or a string to climb, because their tendrils and stems coil round what they touch.

open_questions.q: Does a touch-me-not feel a touch, the way we feel one?
open_questions.why_open: Scientists have measured the electrical signal a touch starts. Many still argue about whether the plant feels it, because nobody can ask a plant.

open_questions.q: How exactly does the growth chemical know to move to the shady side of a shoot?
open_questions.why_open: Scientists have found the light-sensing parts in the tip and the growth chemical, called auxin. How the light sends auxin to the shady side is still being studied.

open_questions.q: How do roots choose between gravity, water and a stone in the way, all at once?
open_questions.why_open: Roots sense many things at the same time. How a root tip weighs them up and decides which way to grow is still being worked out.

maths.problem: In the window test, 12 moong shoots came up. After a day by the window, 9 leaned to the glass and the rest stood straight. How many stood straight? Did most shoots lean?
maths.answer: 3 stood straight. Yes, most leaned: 9 is far more than 3.
maths.explain: 12 take away 9 is 3. 9 shoots leaned and only 3 did not, so most of them leaned.
maths.context: This question is about the window test. You grew moong shoots in the dark, put them by a window, and later turned the cup round.
maths.why_maths: Taking the leaning shoots away from all the shoots tells us how many did not lean, so we can see if the result is clear.

maths.problem: Mala, a girl in Class 2, made a tally of leaflet pairs that folded. Fingertip: |||| |||. Feather: |||. Drop of water: ||||. Gentle blow: |. Which touch folded the most? How many more pairs than the feather?
maths.answer: The fingertip folded the most: 8 pairs. That is 5 more than the feather.
maths.explain: The fingertip has 8 marks, the most. The feather has 3. 8 take away 3 is 5.
maths.context: This question is about the touch-me-not tests. You touched touch-me-not leaves in different ways and counted the pairs of leaflets that folded.
maths.why_maths: A tally shows at a glance which touch the plant responded to most.

maths.problem: A moong root is 2 cm long. It grows 1 cm every day. How long will the root be after 4 days?
maths.explain: 2 cm to start, then 1 cm each day for 4 days: 2 + 1 + 1 + 1 + 1 = 6.
maths.context: This question is about the root box. You laid four moong sprouts in a clear box, with their roots pointing up, down, left and right.
maths.why_maths: Adding on each day's growth lets us predict how long the root will be before we look.

maths.problem: In the turn-the-pot project, Keerthi, a girl in Class 2, counted the leaves facing the window: 2 on day 1, 5 on day 3, 8 on day 5. If the pattern goes on, how many will face the window on day 7?
maths.explain: The number goes up by 3 each time: 2, 5, 8, so next is 11. A real plant may slow down once nearly all the leaves face the light.
maths.context: This question is about the turn-the-pot project. You turned a potted plant round so the leaves faced the room, and counted the leaves facing the window every two days.
maths.why_maths: Spotting the pattern lets us make a guess about the next count, then check it on the real plant.

roots.context: We have watched moong shoots turn to the light, roots turn down, and a touch-me-not fold. Now we ask what these tell us about plants, and about ourselves.

deep_truth.truth: Our straight moong shoots leaned to the window within a day. When we turned the cup, they bent back towards the light. Nobody moved them: each shoot bent by growing more on the shady side. So a plant's shape is a record of where their light came from.
deep_truth.habit: We think of a plant's shape as fixed, like the shape of a chair. But a plant builds their shape day by day from what they sense. A bend in a stem shows where the light was, and a curve in a root shows where down was.
deep_truth.evidence: In the window test, straight shoots leaned to the window within a day. After the cup was turned, their tips turned back, and many stems were left shaped like the letter S. In the root box, a root that pointed up made a hook as it turned down.

three.who_am_i: You sense light, touch and which way is down too. Tiny crystals in your ears tell you where down is, a little like the grains in a root tip.
three.what_is_life: Living beings sense what is around them and respond. A shoot responds to light by bending, and a touch-me-not responds to a touch by folding.
three.what_is_this_world: The world reaches a plant as light, the pull of the Earth, touch and water. Each plant grows their own shape from what reaches them.

roots.thread: Every moong seed in a packet is much the same. Planted in different places, each one grows a different shape, bent by their own light, their own 'down' and their own touches. Everything is conscious, plants too: a shoot senses the light and decides which way to grow. One kind of seed, one Sun and one Earth give countless different plants.

teachings.source: Mahabharata, Shanti Parva, the talk between the sages Bhrigu and Bharadvaja
teachings.teaching: Bhrigu says that trees have senses. They wither in heat, so they feel touch. A creeper winds round a tree and finds the way, so plants can sense where to go. They drink water through their roots.
teachings.link: Our moong shoots found the window, and a climber finds a stick. The old Indian epic asked whether plants sense the world, and gave the same kind of evidence we used: watch what the plant does.

teachings.source: Tattvartha Sutra, chapter 2 (Umasvati, a Jain teacher)
teachings.teaching: Plants are living beings with one sense, the sense of touch. So Jains take great care not to harm them without need.
teachings.link: A touch-me-not shows the sense of touch clearly. Science has since found that plants also sense light, gravity and water. Both say a plant is a living someone who senses.

teachings.source: J.C. Bose, The Nervous Mechanism of Plants (1926)
teachings.teaching: Bose found that a touch on a touch-me-not starts an electrical signal that travels through the plant, like a message along a nerve.
teachings.link: When you touched one leaflet, the folding ran along the leaf. That running fold is the signal Bose measured in Kolkata.

science.text: A shoot bends to light because a growth chemical, auxin, gathers on the shady side and makes it grow longer.
Whether a plant's sensing comes with feeling, the way ours does, is still argued about.

other_view.view: They explain bending, root turning and folding fully by chemicals, water and growth. They call these automatic responses, and do not say the plant decides or remembers.

practice.title: Turn to the light
practice.say: Sit near a window and close your eyes. Keep them closed. Can you feel which side the light and warmth come from? Slowly turn your face towards it, like a shoot. Stay still and breathe slowly three times. Now open your eyes. Were you facing the window?
practice.kid: Sit near a window. Close your eyes. Feel where the light comes from. Turn your face to it slowly. Breathe three times. Open your eyes.

ask: If your shape grew from everything you sensed, what would it show?
A touch-me-not senses touch, and you do too. Is a plant's touch like yours?
Who decides which way the moong shoot grows: the shoot, the light, or both?
